title: Revenue, margin, and product-performance analysis
objective: Compute revenue, cost of goods, gross margin ($ and %) and refund-adjusted figures by product, category and year, find dead stock, and rank products by their contribution to total margin.
context: Revenue is vanity, margin is sanity. Finance has loaded unit costs (product_costs) and wants to know which products and categories actually make money after costs and refunds, which catalog items have never sold, and how concentrated margin is in a few hero products.

exercises.title: Product gross margin
exercises.question: Finance wants revenue, cost and margin for every product that sold.
exercises.prompt: Use lines of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price); cogs = SUM(quantity * unit_cost) with unit_cost from product_costs; gross_margin = revenue - cogs. Return product_id, product_name, units_sold (SUM(quantity)), revenue, cogs, gross_margin (each rounded to 2) and margin_pct (100.0 * gross_margin / revenue, 0–100 scale, rounded to 1 decimal). One row per product with sales.
hints: Join order lines to product_costs on product_id; cost is quantity * unit_cost.
Compute margin_pct from the summed revenue and summed margin — not as AVG of line percentages.

SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, SUM(oi.quantity), ROUND(SUM(qty*price),2), ROUND(SUM(qty*unit_cost),2), ROUND(SUM(qty*price) - SUM(qty*unit_cost),2), ROUND(100.0*(...)/SUM(qty*price),1) ... GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name;
exercises.why: The product P&L is the foundation of pricing and assortment decisions — high revenue with thin margin is a different problem from low revenue with fat margin.

recall.q: Why compute margin % as SUM(margin)/SUM(revenue) rather than AVG(line margin %)?
recall.a: AVG of ratios weights a $5 line the same as a $500 line; the ratio of sums is revenue-weighted, which is what finance means.

exercises.title: Category performance
exercises.question: Which categories generate the most gross margin?
exercises.prompt: Same definitions as 40.1 (valid orders; gross_margin = revenue - quantity*unit_cost). Return category ('Uncategorized' when NULL), products_sold (distinct products with sales), revenue, gross_margin (rounded to 2) and margin_pct (100.0 * gross_margin / revenue, rounded to 1 decimal). Order by gross_margin descending, then category.
hints: Same joins as 40.1, but GROUP BY category.
Line margin = quantity * (unit_price - unit_cost); COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) for products_sold.
... GROUP BY COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized') ORDER BY gross_margin DESC, category;
exercises.why: Category managers are measured on margin dollars; margin % tells you whether growth there is healthy.

recall.q: Is quantity*(unit_price - unit_cost) summed the same as SUM(revenue) - SUM(cost)?
recall.a: Yes — summation distributes over subtraction, so both give the same margin.

exercises.title: Net of refunds
exercises.question: Returns eat into margin. Show each product's refunds and margin after refunds.
exercises.prompt: Valid orders only (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Per product with sales: revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price), refunds = SUM(returns.refund_amount) for that product's returned lines (0 if none), net_revenue = revenue - refunds, cogs = SUM(quantity * unit_cost), net_margin = net_revenue - cogs (we assume returned goods are written off, so cost stays). Return product_id, revenue, refunds, net_revenue, net_margin (all rounded to 2) for products that had at least one refund. Order by refunds descending, then product_id.
hints: Refunds attach to order lines (order_item_id). LEFT JOIN them so lines without a return keep their revenue.
Pre-aggregate returns per order_item_id so a line can never be duplicated by the join; COALESCE missing refunds to 0.
lines CTE (order_item_id, product_id, revenue, cogs) LEFT JOIN refunds CTE ON order_item_id, GROUP BY product_id HAVING SUM(COALESCE(refund,0)) > 0 ORDER BY refunds DESC, product_id;
exercises.why: A product with great gross margin can be a loser after returns. Pre-aggregating the 'many' side before joining is the habit that prevents fan-out double counting.

recall.q: Why LEFT JOIN returns rather than INNER JOIN when computing net revenue per product?
recall.a: An inner join would keep only returned lines and drop all the revenue from lines that weren't returned.

exercises.title: Products never sold
exercises.question: Merchandising wants the catalog items that have never sold, with the margin they would make at list price.
exercises.prompt: A product is 'never sold' if it appears on no line of a valid order (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return product_id, product_name, category, list_price, unit_cost and potential_unit_margin (list_price - unit_cost, rounded to 2). Order by product_id.
hints: 'Never sold' is an anti-join: products with no matching valid sale.
Put the status filter INSIDE the NOT EXISTS subquery (join order_items to orders there).

SELECT ... FROM products p JOIN product_costs pc ... WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON ... WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id AND o.order_status IN (...)) ORDER BY p.product_id;
exercises.why: Dead stock ties up cash and shelf space. Note the Smart Watch would carry the biggest unit margin of all — maybe it's a merchandising problem, not a product problem.

recall.q: If you use LEFT JOIN ... WHERE oi.order_item_id IS NULL for 'never sold', where must the status filter go?
recall.a: Into the ON clause (or a pre-filtered subquery) — in WHERE it would turn the anti-join back into an inner join.

exercises.title: Margin contribution (Pareto)
exercises.question: How concentrated is our margin? Do 20% of products make 80% of the margin?
exercises.prompt: Gross margin per product = SUM(quantity * (unit_price - unit_cost)) over lines of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return product_id, product_name, gross_margin (rounded 2), pct_of_total_margin (product margin as a 0–100 percentage of total gross margin, rounded to 1) and cumulative_pct (running total of the percentage, products taken in order of gross_margin descending then product_id, computed from unrounded values and rounded to 1). Order by gross_margin descending, then product_id.
hints: Per-product margin in a CTE; then two windows: the grand total and a running total.
Grand total: SUM(gross_margin) OVER (). Running: SUM(gross_margin) OVER (ORDER BY gross_margin DESC, product_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
ROUND(100.0 * gross_margin / SUM(gross_margin) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total_margin, ROUND(100.0 * <running sum> / SUM(gross_margin) OVER (), 1) AS cumulative_pct
exercises.why: Pareto curves decide where to focus: protect the top contributors' availability and price, rationalise the long tail.

recall.q: Why compute cumulative_pct from unrounded values?
recall.a: Summing rounded percentages accumulates rounding error, so the curve may not end exactly at 100.

exercises.snowflake: RATIO_TO_REPORT(gross_margin) OVER () * 100 AS pct_of_total_margin; the running share uses the same SUM ... OVER (ORDER BY ... ROWS ...) frame.

exercises.title: Yearly P&L after refunds
exercises.question: The CFO wants a two-line P&L: 2024 vs 2025 revenue, refunds, cost and net margin.
exercises.prompt: Valid orders only (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')); attribute everything to the year of the ORDER date (not the return date). Return order_year ('YYYY'), revenue (SUM(quantity * unit_price)), refunds (SUM(refund_amount) of returned lines, 0 if none), cogs (SUM(quantity * unit_cost)), net_margin (revenue - refunds - cogs), all rounded to 2, and net_margin_pct (100.0 * net_margin / (revenue - refunds), rounded to 1 decimal). Order by order_year.
hints: Line-level CTE with order_year, revenue and cogs; refunds pre-aggregated per order_item_id.
LEFT JOIN refunds to lines, GROUP BY order_year, then compute margin and % in an outer SELECT from the unrounded sums.
yearly CTE: SUM(revenue), SUM(COALESCE(refund,0)), SUM(cogs) GROUP BY order_year; final: ROUND(revenue - refunds - cogs, 2), ROUND(100.0*(revenue - refunds - cogs)/(revenue - refunds), 1).
exercises.why: Attribution choices (order date vs return date) change the numbers; stating them explicitly is part of the deliverable.

recall.q: Name two ways to attribute a refund to a period.
recall.a: By the original order date (cohort-style, used here) or by the return/refund date (cash/accounting view).

exercises.snowflake: YEAR(o.order_date) AS order_year; DIV0(net_margin, revenue - refunds) * 100 for the percentage.

worked_example.question: What were total revenue, cost and gross margin across all valid orders?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2)                  AS revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * pc.unit_cost), 2)                    AS cogs,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * (oi.unit_price - pc.unit_cost)), 2)  AS gross_margin,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(oi.quantity * (oi.unit_price - pc.unit_cost))
             / SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 1)                 AS margin_pct
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN product_costs AS pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned');
worked_example.explanation: Every product has a cost row, so the inner join to product_costs loses nothing. margin_pct is computed from the two sums — the revenue-weighted margin — not as an average of per-line percentages.

recipe:
**Recipe: margin analysis in 5 moves**

1. **Line-level facts** (valid orders only, `order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')`):
   revenue = `quantity * unit_price`; cost (COGS) = `quantity * unit_cost` from `product_costs`.
2. **Gross margin** = revenue − cost; **margin %** = 100.0 × margin / revenue (0–100 scale).
3. **Refunds** live in `returns` (one row per returned order line). Aggregate them separately and join on
   `order_item_id` — or pre-aggregate per product — so the join cannot multiply line rows.
   Net revenue = revenue − refunds.
4. **Roll up** with GROUP BY product / category / year. Compute percentages *from the sums*, never by
   averaging line-level percentages.
5. **Contribution:** share of total = `margin / SUM(margin) OVER ()`; Pareto curve = running sum of that
   share ordered by margin DESC.

```sql
SELECT p.category,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)                     AS revenue,
       SUM(oi.quantity * (oi.unit_price - pc.unit_cost))    AS gross_margin
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items  oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id
JOIN products     p  ON p.product_id  = oi.product_id
JOIN product_costs pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY p.category;
```
snowflake_notes:
The SQL is the same in Snowflake; useful additions:

- `DIV0(margin, revenue)` returns 0 instead of an error when revenue is 0 (`DIV0NULL` also treats NULL as 0).
- `RATIO_TO_REPORT(gross_margin) OVER ()` for contribution share (0–1).
- `QUALIFY` for "top N products per category":

```sql
SELECT p.category, p.product_name,
       SUM(oi.quantity * (oi.unit_price - pc.unit_cost)) AS gross_margin
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi   ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p       ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
JOIN product_costs pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY 1, 2
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category ORDER BY gross_margin DESC, p.product_name) <= 3;
```

- Use `NUMBER(38,2)` (fixed-point) for money in Snowflake tables; floating-point sums like 96.89999999 are
  a SQLite/FLOAT artifact — round at the end, not in the middle.
common_mistakes: Using products.list_price instead of order_items.unit_price for revenue.
Averaging line-level margin percentages instead of dividing summed margin by summed revenue.
Joining returns without pre-aggregation or with an INNER JOIN — losing or duplicating revenue.
Putting the valid-status filter in the WHERE of a LEFT JOIN anti-join, which silently turns it into an inner join.
Rounding intermediate values and then summing them; round only the final outputs.
Forgetting the NULL category (product 20) — it vanishes or shows as NULL unless you COALESCE it.
recall: Define gross margin and margin % as used in this lesson.
Gross margin = revenue − quantity × unit_cost; margin % = 100 × gross margin / revenue.
How do you compute each product's share of total margin in one pass?
gross_margin / SUM(gross_margin) OVER () (× 100), or RATIO_TO_REPORT in Snowflake.
Which products have never sold, and how do you find them?
Products 23, 24, 25 — via NOT EXISTS (or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL) against lines of valid orders.
